e-21546.knowledge_point: Constructing the Formulas for Variation of Parameters
e-21546.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form $\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \mathbf{u}(t),$ where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for $\mathbf x_p(t)$ is given below. 

$\textrm{L1}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \mathbf{u}(t)$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{x}'_p(t) = \Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) + \Phi' \mathbf{u}(t)$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\:$ $\Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) + \Phi' \mathbf{u}(t) = A \Phi \mathbf{u}(t) + \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\:$ $\Phi' = A \Phi$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\:$ $\Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{u}'(t) = \Phi^{-1}(t) \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L7}{:}\:$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t$

$\textrm{L8}{:}\:$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t$

Fill in the blanks with the correct reasons to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L4}$ follows from the fact that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/81e146c6f6297f8f30340d63ddaec02efe3d6442005f5852a70d5be22ceed764.png) matrix.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L6}$ follows from line $\textrm{L5}$ by  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/09febb48bb00d22caebf088103181b5db6377befccad18f1370718351cc91e9d.png) both sides of the equation.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\textrm{L7}$ into ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/9be3bba9e4f49ae67d635fe7b6260607d3e776f03baeaf8d5a10d650e0b0b987.png)
e-21546.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\textrm{L4}.$ Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t) =A\mathbf{x}(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $\mathbf{c}(t)$ of $\Phi$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
\mathbf{c}'(t) =A\mathbf{c}(t),
$$

where $\mathbf{c}'(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $\Phi.$ As a result, this means that $\Phi' = A \Phi.$ Therefore, $\textrm{L4}$ follows from the fact that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/f3cf7b9339acd3d9b370c67a182509bff354728494afda00e2e991f3a09996af.png) matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\textrm{L5}$ and $\textrm{L6}.$ Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $\Phi$ is invertible. Therefore, $\textrm{L6}$ follows from $\textrm{L5}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/8ba4d14f89d4c90c90f84e0618b0cf8dedadbf2c3989cc9533e44590100357d1.png) both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L1},$ $\textrm{L7},$ and $\textrm{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t
$$

from $\textrm{L7}$ into $\textrm{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\textrm{L7}$ into  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/4d1fa76e9619981c1b36c457c5247dad023bdbb7f7810fdc9e5b9105028c4e22.png)

e-21547.knowledge_point: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs
e-21547.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/2b22742201ba6932de40a628419faef0405bc8ae0ad26814bc7ca515455e3e5c.png)
Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute $\Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t)$ and the particular solution $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ of the system.
e-21547.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/0c7accec33fc7c9d6b2a228c8ec4bcc454f687be7f96ab615b3b818f82fb8cc8.png)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2{e}^{-4t})-2{e}^{-4t}\cdot {e}^{3t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{t} \\ -\frac{17}{10}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{17}{10}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-21548.knowledge_point: Solving an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters
e-21548.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/bc92d310e939c8688ab770a51107d1218d5b8878a877d7b3a64af770d002a9ca.png)
Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

| ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/860251c7cc4c1259c4660b41aae1f3e0b0177e13c9372dd941422040f0f7e5ee.png) |  | $\boxed{\rule{0pt}{1.3em}\phantom{xxxxxxxx}}$ |  | . |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $0$ |  |  |  |
e-21548.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_c(t) + \mathbf{x}_p(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_c(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/e8db6a28a4671312259595de0609cefb8db0d5fc441e122885335e1165e0cd22.png)

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/742a0ea79220f0dc0055918b611393d69518bc5c73ef9b41b6fd068c8c75ad4c.png)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-4t}-0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 0\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=2t$ and $\text{d}v=e^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, the integrand is zero, so the integral is zero.

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Because Φ is a fundamental matrix, each column solves the homogeneous system, so Φ′=AΦ. Substituting L4 into L3 cancels the AΦu terms and gives L5. Integrating L6 gives L7, and substituting L7 into L1 gives L8.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-4}} into $\text{L1}.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), i.e., by substituting any column c(t) of Φ into the homogeneous system, we get c′(t)=Ac(t), where c′(t) is the corresponding column of derivatives in Φ. content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Formulas for Variation of Parameters
content.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-4}} into $\text{L1}.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

after.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-4}} matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. To get L2, we are differentiating with respect to t both sides of the equation in L1: xp′(t)=(Φu(t))′xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

  • Next, we consider lines L1, L2, and L3. Let's substitute xp(t)=Φu(t) from L1 and xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t) from L2 into the initial system of ODEs: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) Therefore, L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into initial system of ODEs.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by pre-multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Formulas for Variation of Parameters
content.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-4}} matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

after.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-4}} .
after.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-4}} .
content.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

content.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into {{field-4}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

decision.explanation: Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns satisfy the homogeneous system, giving Φ′=AΦ. Pre-multiplying Φu′=f by Φ⁻¹ gives u′=Φ⁻¹f. Integrating this equation gives L7.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.
after.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{4t}-0\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 2{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -8{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

after.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}12t \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}12t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 8t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t} \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=8t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=8\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =8t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 8\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}+\int 8\,{e}^{-t}\text{d}t \\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}-8{e}^{2t} \\  & =-8{e}^{-t}(1+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ -8{e}^{-t}(1+t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(1-2t)-16(1+t) \\ 2(1-2t)-8(1+t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18t-15 \\ -12t-6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}12t \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}12t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 8t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For the first component, let $u=-4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t} \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=8t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=8\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =8t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 8\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}+\int 8\,{e}^{-t}\text{d}t \\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}-8{e}^{2t} \\  & =-8{e}^{-t}(1+t).\end{aligned}

$$

Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{t}-5{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -5{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -5{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & -5{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t} \\ -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}t \\ 3t\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2t{e}^{2t} \\ 3t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-2t{e}^{2t} \\ 3t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-2t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-2\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-2\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-t{e}^{2t}+\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ 3{e}^{t}(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}(1-2t)+6(t-1) \\ 6(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}4t-5 \\ 6t-6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
